children.text: A simplified automobile accelerometer uses a movable capacitor plate and springs. Ignore gravity as a force on the apparatus. All plates have area A, gaps are much smaller than plate dimensions, and air permittivity is \(\epsilon_0\). For part 1 a movable plate on one spring k faces a fixed plate. Its unstretched separation is d and \(C_0=\epsilon_0A/d\). The isolated plates carry fixed charges \(\pm Q\). For parts 2 and 3 a mass M and a negligible-mass central plate are supported between two fixed plates by two springs, each of constant k. The fixed plates are held at \(+V\) and \(-V\). At zero acceleration each gap is d. Let \(x>0\) mean a central-plate displacement towards the \(+V\) electrode. In state alpha the central plate is grounded. In state beta it is connected to ground through an initially uncharged capacitor \(C_S\). During parts 2 and 3 assume equilibrium relative to the accelerating car.

nodes.alt: Original fixed and movable capacitor plates with spring stiffness k and initial gap d.

children.text: Find the force magnitude between the two isolated capacitor plates.
Find the movable-plate displacement towards the fixed plate.
Find the potential difference after mechanical equilibrium.
Find total electrical plus spring energy at equilibrium.

nodes.alt: Original central plate and mass M between two sprung fixed plates, voltage sources, switch and signal capacitor Cs.

children.text: In state alpha find the charge magnitudes on the \(+V\)-side and \(-V\)-side capacitors as functions of x.
Find the signed electrical force towards the positive electrode.
Write the combined spring and electric force as \(-k_{eff}x\), and find \(k_{eff}\).
For positive lag x towards the positive electrode, find the magnitude of the car acceleration away from that electrode.
In state beta find the central-plate potential \(V_S\) relative to ground.
Neglect \(x^2\) against \(d^2\) and simplify the preceding result.

Now abandon the equilibrium assumption for a sudden braking event. Use \(d=1.0\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(A=2.5\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), \(k=4.2\times10^3\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(\epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{SI}\), \(V=12\,\mathrm V\), \(M=0.15\,\mathrm{kg}\), and ignore friction. Find electric-force magnitude divided by total spring-force magnitude.
A car initially at constant velocity suddenly acquires constant acceleration of magnitude a. Find maximum displacement of the movable plate.
In state beta the air bag triggers at \(V_S=0.15\,\mathrm V\). Choose \(C_S\) so it does not trigger for constant braking acceleration below \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), but reaches the threshold at g.
Estimate head-to-steering-wheel distance, then estimate time to contact when the car decelerates at g but the head initially keeps its constant velocity.
Find the trigger time at deceleration g and compare with the contact-time estimate. Assume the air bag opens instantaneously.

statement.text:
Capacitive accelerometer
A simplified automobile accelerometer uses a movable capacitor plate and springs. Ignore gravity as a force on the apparatus. All plates have area A, gaps are much smaller than plate dimensions, and air permittivity is \(\epsilon_0\). For part 1 a movable plate on one spring k faces a fixed plate. Its unstretched separation is d and \(C_0=\epsilon_0A/d\). The isolated plates carry fixed charges \(\pm Q\). For parts 2 and 3 a mass M and a negligible-mass central plate are supported between two fixed plates by two springs, each of constant k. The fixed plates are held at \(+V\) and \(-V\). At zero acceleration each gap is d. Let \(x>0\) mean a central-plate displacement towards the \(+V\) electrode. In state alpha the central plate is grounded. In state beta it is connected to ground through an initially uncharged capacitor \(C_S\). During parts 2 and 3 assume equilibrium relative to the accelerating car.

1.1. Fixed-charge attraction
Find the force magnitude between the two isolated capacitor plates.
1.2. Equilibrium displacement
Find the movable-plate displacement towards the fixed plate.
1.3. Equilibrium voltage
Find the potential difference after mechanical equilibrium.
1.4. Capacitance ratio
Find \(C/C_0\).
1.5. Stored energy
Find total electrical plus spring energy at equilibrium.
2.1. Grounded-plate capacitor charges

In state alpha find the charge magnitudes on the \(+V\)-side and \(-V\)-side capacitors as functions of x.
2.2. Net electrical force
Find the signed electrical force towards the positive electrode.
2.3. Small-displacement force
Keep only terms linear in \(x/d\).
2.4. Effective stiffness
Write the combined spring and electric force as \(-k_{eff}x\), and find \(k_{eff}\).
2.5. Acceleration and lag
For positive lag x towards the positive electrode, find the magnitude of the car acceleration away from that electrode.
3.1. Series-capacitor signal
In state beta find the central-plate potential \(V_S\) relative to ground.
3.2. Linear voltage signal
Neglect \(x^2\) against \(d^2\) and simplify the preceding result.
4.1. Negligible electrical correction
Now abandon the equilibrium assumption for a sudden braking event. Use \(d=1.0\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(A=2.5\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), \(k=4.2\times10^3\,\mathrm{N/m}\), \(\epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{SI}\), \(V=12\,\mathrm V\), \(M=0.15\,\mathrm{kg}\), and ignore friction. Find electric-force magnitude divided by total spring-force magnitude.
4.2. Maximum braking displacement
A car initially at constant velocity suddenly acquires constant acceleration of magnitude a. Find maximum displacement of the movable plate.
4.3. Threshold capacitor
In state beta the air bag triggers at \(V_S=0.15\,\mathrm V\). Choose \(C_S\) so it does not trigger for constant braking acceleration below \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), but reaches the threshold at g.
4.4. Time until head contact
Estimate head-to-steering-wheel distance, then estimate time to contact when the car decelerates at g but the head initially keeps its constant velocity.
4.5. Activation time and comparison
Find the trigger time at deceleration g and compare with the contact-time estimate. Assume the air bag opens instantaneously.

children.text: Only the other plate's field acts on a given plate. Its field is \(Q/(2\epsilon_0A)\), so \(F_E=Q^2/(2\epsilon_0A)\), independent of gap.
Balance spring and electrical forces: \(kx=F_E\), hence \(x=Q^2/(2\epsilon_0Ak)\).
The final gap is \(d-x\). Thus \[V=\frac{Qd}{\epsilon_0A}\left(1-\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0Akd}\right).\] This requires the gap to remain positive.
The gaps are \(d-x\) and \(d+x\). Therefore \(Q_+=\epsilon_0AV/(d-x)\), \(Q_-=\epsilon_0AV/(d+x)\). The central faces carry opposite signs.
The two attractions oppose each other: \[F_E=\frac{\epsilon_0AV^2}{2}\left[\frac1{(d-x)^2}-\frac1{(d+x)^2}\right].\]
Binomial expansion gives \(F_E\simeq2\epsilon_0AV^2x/d^3\). The electrical force is destabilizing.
Both springs supply restoring force, totalling \(-2kx\). Hence \[k_{eff}=2k-2\epsilon_0AV^2/d^3.\] Stable centring requires this coefficient to be positive.

In the car frame, inertial force balances the restoring force: \(Ma=k_{eff}x\). Thus \[a=\frac{2x}{M}(k-\epsilon_0AV^2/d^3).\] The signed acceleration in the +x direction is minus this value. This states explicitly the coordinate convention behind the sign in the source.

The isolated central conductor and its connected capacitor plate have zero net charge. With \(C_+=\epsilon_0A/(d-x)\), \(C_-=\epsilon_0A/(d+x)\), charge balance gives \(C_+(V_S-V)+C_-(V_S+V)+C_SV_S=0\). Therefore \[V_S=\frac{2\epsilon_0AVx}{C_S(d^2-x^2)+2\epsilon_0Ad}.\]
The ratio is \(\epsilon_0AV^2/(kd^3)=7.6\times10^{-9}\). Thus electric forces can be neglected in the transient mechanical motion. The same smallness holds in state beta.
In the accelerating frame the displacement obeys \(M\ddot x+2kx=Ma\), starting with zero displacement and relative velocity. Thus \[x(t)=\frac{Ma}{2k}[1-\cos(\sqrt{2k/M}\,t)],\qquad x_{max}=Ma/k.\]
At the first displacement maximum, \(x_{max}=Mg/k\). Combine with 3.2 to get \[C_S=\frac{2\epsilon_0A}{d}\left(\frac{VMg}{kV_Sd}-1\right)=8.0\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm F.\]

For an estimated gap \(l\), the initial relative velocity is zero and closing distance is \(gt_1^2/2\). Thus \(t_1=\sqrt{2l/g}\). A plausible \(l=0.4\) to \(1\,\mathrm m\) gives \(t_1\simeq0.3\) to \(0.5\,\mathrm s\). This estimate depends on the chosen gap and is self-review.

The threshold is reached at the first displacement maximum, half a mechanical period: \[t_2=\pi\sqrt{M/(2k)}=0.013\,\mathrm s.\] It is much shorter than the estimated \(0.3\) to \(0.5\,\mathrm s\), so this idealized model triggers in time. It omits the real inflation time.

solution.text:
Capacitive accelerometer
1.1. Fixed-charge attraction
Only the other plate's field acts on a given plate. Its field is \(Q/(2\epsilon_0A)\), so \(F_E=Q^2/(2\epsilon_0A)\), independent of gap.
1.2. Equilibrium displacement
Balance spring and electrical forces: \(kx=F_E\), hence \(x=Q^2/(2\epsilon_0Ak)\).
1.3. Equilibrium voltage
The final gap is \(d-x\). Thus \[V=\frac{Qd}{\epsilon_0A}\left(1-\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0Akd}\right).\] This requires the gap to remain positive.
1.4. Capacitance ratio
\(C=\epsilon_0A/(d-x)\), so \[C/C_0=\left(1-\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0Akd}\right)^{-1}.\]
1.5. Stored energy
\(U=Q^2(d-x)/(2\epsilon_0A)+kx^2/2\). Substitution gives \[U=\frac{Q^2d}{2\epsilon_0A}\left(1-\frac{Q^2}{4\epsilon_0Akd}\right).\]
2.1. Grounded-plate capacitor charges
The gaps are \(d-x\) and \(d+x\). Therefore \(Q_+=\epsilon_0AV/(d-x)\), \(Q_-=\epsilon_0AV/(d+x)\). The central faces carry opposite signs.
2.2. Net electrical force
The two attractions oppose each other: \[F_E=\frac{\epsilon_0AV^2}{2}\left[\frac1{(d-x)^2}-\frac1{(d+x)^2}\right].\]
2.3. Small-displacement force
Binomial expansion gives \(F_E\simeq2\epsilon_0AV^2x/d^3\). The electrical force is destabilizing.
2.4. Effective stiffness
Both springs supply restoring force, totalling \(-2kx\). Hence \[k_{eff}=2k-2\epsilon_0AV^2/d^3.\] Stable centring requires this coefficient to be positive.
2.5. Acceleration and lag
In the car frame, inertial force balances the restoring force: \(Ma=k_{eff}x\). Thus \[a=\frac{2x}{M}(k-\epsilon_0AV^2/d^3).\] The signed acceleration in the +x direction is minus this value. This states explicitly the coordinate convention behind the sign in the source.
3.1. Series-capacitor signal
The isolated central conductor and its connected capacitor plate have zero net charge. With \(C_+=\epsilon_0A/(d-x)\), \(C_-=\epsilon_0A/(d+x)\), charge balance gives \(C_+(V_S-V)+C_-(V_S+V)+C_SV_S=0\). Therefore \[V_S=\frac{2\epsilon_0AVx}{C_S(d^2-x^2)+2\epsilon_0Ad}.\]
3.2. Linear voltage signal
\[V_S\simeq\frac{2\epsilon_0AVx}{d^2C_S+2\epsilon_0Ad}.\]
4.1. Negligible electrical correction
The ratio is \(\epsilon_0AV^2/(kd^3)=7.6\times10^{-9}\). Thus electric forces can be neglected in the transient mechanical motion. The same smallness holds in state beta.
4.2. Maximum braking displacement
In the accelerating frame the displacement obeys \(M\ddot x+2kx=Ma\), starting with zero displacement and relative velocity. Thus \[x(t)=\frac{Ma}{2k}[1-\cos(\sqrt{2k/M}\,t)],\qquad x_{max}=Ma/k.\]
4.3. Threshold capacitor
At the first displacement maximum, \(x_{max}=Mg/k\). Combine with 3.2 to get \[C_S=\frac{2\epsilon_0A}{d}\left(\frac{VMg}{kV_Sd}-1\right)=8.0\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm F.\]
4.4. Time until head contact
For an estimated gap \(l\), the initial relative velocity is zero and closing distance is \(gt_1^2/2\). Thus \(t_1=\sqrt{2l/g}\). A plausible \(l=0.4\) to \(1\,\mathrm m\) gives \(t_1\simeq0.3\) to \(0.5\,\mathrm s\). This estimate depends on the chosen gap and is self-review.
4.5. Activation time and comparison
The threshold is reached at the first displacement maximum, half a mechanical period: \[t_2=\pi\sqrt{M/(2k)}=0.013\,\mathrm s.\] It is much shorter than the estimated \(0.3\) to \(0.5\,\mathrm s\), so this idealized model triggers in time. It omits the real inflation time.
